blocks.topic: Best Interest of the Child Standard
blocks.conclusion_template: The best interest of the child is the paramount standard in all custody determinations. Courts weigh statutory factors including emotional ties, parental capacity, stability of home environment, the child's adjustment to community and school, mental and physical health of all parties, and any history of domestic violence or substance abuse. No single factor is dispositive; the totality of circumstances governs.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. STATUTORY FACTOR ANALYSIS: Enumerate all best-interest factors under applicable state family code. 2. EVIDENCE MAPPING: Map available evidence to each factor with strength rating. 3. WEIGHTING: Courts give heightened weight to domestic violence, substance abuse, and child's expressed preference (age-dependent). 4. STABILITY PREFERENCE: Status quo bias favors maintaining existing arrangements absent compelling reason to change. 5. PARENTAL COOPERATION: Willingness to foster relationship with other parent is a significant factor in most jurisdictions.
key_factors: Emotional ties between child and each parent
Parental capacity and willingness to provide
Child's adjustment to home, school, community
Mental and physical health of parties
Child's preference if of sufficient age and maturity
Willingness to encourage relationship with other parent

primary_authority.relevance: Best interest is primary consideration in custody
Best interest factors for joint managing conservatorship
Model best-interest factors adopted by majority of states

counter_arguments: Factor weighting is inherently subjective and varies by judge
Status quo bias can perpetuate arrangements born of unequal bargaining
Child preference evidence is unreliable below age 12 in most jurisdictions
Best-interest standard gives little predictive guidance to parties negotiating settlement

blocks.conclusion_template: In community property jurisdictions (AZ, CA, ID, LA, NV, NM, TX, WA, WI), all property acquired during marriage is presumed community unless proven separate by clear and convincing evidence. Courts divide community property in a manner that is 'just and right' (TX) or 'substantially equal' (CA), considering factors including fault, disparity in earning capacity, custody of children, and waste of community assets.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. CHARACTERIZATION: Classify each asset as community or separate. Separate property = owned before marriage, acquired by gift/inheritance, or personal injury recovery. 2. TRACING: If commingled, trace inception of title and apply community-out-first rule. 3. REIMBURSEMENT: Calculate reimbursement claims for community funds used on separate property and vice versa. 4. VALUATION: Determine fair market value as of date of division. 5. DIVISION: Divide community estate considering statutory factors. Disproportionate division requires justification on the record.
key_factors: Date of acquisition relative to marriage

primary_authority.relevance: Clear and convincing standard for separate property

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Mix, 14 Cal.3d 604 (1975)
primary_authority.relevance: Substantially equal division required in CA

counter_arguments: Tracing evidence is often incomplete making characterization uncertain
Just and right standard gives courts wide discretion with limited appellate review
Date of separation disputes affect characterization
Inception of title vs transmutation theories may yield different results

blocks.conclusion_template: In equitable distribution states (41 states + DC), courts divide marital property in a fair and equitable manner, which need not be equal. Courts consider duration of marriage, each spouse's economic circumstances, contributions (monetary and non-monetary including homemaking), age and health, custody arrangements, tax consequences, and any prenuptial agreements. Separate property (pre-marital, gifts, inheritances) is generally excluded unless commingled.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. IDENTIFY MARITAL vs SEPARATE: Date of marriage to date of separation/filing. 2. VALUE ALL MARITAL ASSETS: FMV at date of distribution or trial. 3. APPLY STATUTORY FACTORS: Duration, contributions, earning capacity, age/health. 4. CONSIDER TAX IMPACT: Capital gains, retirement account distribution, property transfer. 5. CRAFT DISTRIBUTION: Need not be 50/50; must be equitable based on totality of factors.
key_factors: Each party's income and earning capacity
Contribution to marital estate including homemaking
Dissipation or waste of marital assets

primary_authority.relevance: Equitable distribution factors in New York
Enhanced earning capacity as marital property (NY)

counter_arguments: Equitable does not mean equal giving courts wide discretion
Valuation dates vary by jurisdiction creating uncertainty
Non-monetary contributions are inherently subjective to value
Enhanced earning capacity treatment varies dramatically by state

blocks.topic: Child Support Guidelines — Income Shares Model
blocks.conclusion_template: The majority of states use the Income Shares Model for child support, which estimates the amount parents would have spent on the child if the household were intact and apportions that amount between parents based on their respective incomes. Gross income includes wages, salary, commissions, bonuses, self-employment income, dividends, pensions, and imputed income for voluntarily unemployed or underemployed parents. Deviations require specific findings on the record.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. DETERMINE GROSS INCOME: Both parents. Include all sources per statutory definition. 2. ADJUST FOR ALLOWABLE DEDUCTIONS: Taxes, pre-existing support orders, health insurance for the child. 3. COMBINE INCOMES: Look up basic child support obligation on schedule/table. 4. APPORTION: Each parent's share proportional to their percentage of combined income. 5. CREDIT: Offset for health insurance, extraordinary medical, childcare costs. 6. DEVIATION ANALYSIS: Only for specific statutory reasons documented on the record.
key_factors: Gross income of both parents from all sources

primary_authority.relevance: Net resources defined for child support

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Bush, 191 Ill. App. 3d 249 (1989)
primary_authority.relevance: All income sources included in support calculation

counter_arguments: Guideline amounts may be inadequate for high-income families
Income shares model may not reflect actual expenditure patterns
Self-employment income is easily manipulated
Imputed income determinations are inherently speculative

blocks.conclusion_template: Spousal support is awarded based on statutory factors including the duration of marriage, each spouse's financial resources and earning capacity, age and health, contributions to the other spouse's education or career, and the standard of living during marriage. Modern trend favors rehabilitative support (time-limited) over permanent support, except in long-duration marriages where self-sufficiency is unlikely. Amount and duration are within the court's discretion subject to statutory caps in some jurisdictions.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. THRESHOLD: Does requesting spouse meet eligibility criteria (e.g., inability to meet minimum needs, marriage duration thresholds)? 2. AMOUNT: Consider statutory caps, standard of living, needs vs ability to pay. 3. DURATION: Short marriage = rehabilitative; long marriage = potentially indefinite. 4. TYPE: Temporary, rehabilitative, reimbursement, or permanent. 5. MODIFIABILITY: Unless contractual (non-modifiable by agreement), support is modifiable upon material change.
key_factors: Each spouse's earning capacity and education
Contribution to other spouse's career or education

primary_authority.relevance: Texas spousal maintenance eligibility and factors

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Smith, 990 P.2d 342 (Or. App. 1999)
primary_authority.relevance: Standard of living as spousal support benchmark

counter_arguments: Support duration caps may be inadequate for displaced homemakers
Earning capacity imputation for long-absent spouse is speculative
Standard of living measurement is subjective
Tax treatment changes under TCJA 2017 shifted economics of support

blocks.conclusion_template: Prenuptial agreements are enforceable if they meet requirements of the Uniform Premarital Agreement Act (UPAA) or state equivalent: voluntary execution, fair disclosure of assets, and terms not unconscionable at enforcement. Procedural defenses include duress, lack of independent counsel, inadequate time to review, and insufficient disclosure. Substantive unconscionability is measured at time of enforcement, not execution, in most jurisdictions.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. FORMATION: Written, signed before marriage, voluntary. 2. DISCLOSURE: Full and fair disclosure of assets and obligations. 3. INDEPENDENT COUNSEL: Both parties had opportunity to consult counsel. 4. VOLUNTARINESS: No duress, undue influence, or fraud. 5. UNCONSCIONABILITY: Test at time of enforcement. Consider changed circumstances. 6. SCOPE: Cannot adversely affect child support or custody rights.
key_factors: Whether both parties had independent counsel
Whether terms are unconscionable at enforcement
Compliance with UPAA or state requirements
Whether agreement waives child support (void if so)

primary_authority.relevance: Prenups enforceable without full understanding of rights waived

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Bonds, 24 Cal.4th 1 (2000)

counter_arguments: Unconscionability timing (execution vs enforcement) varies by state
Independent counsel requirement not universal
Disclosure adequacy is fact-intensive
Changed circumstances may render agreement unjust

blocks.conclusion_template: Modification of a custody order requires proof of a material and substantial change in circumstances since the prior order, and that modification serves the child's best interest. The movant bears the burden on both elements. Courts apply a higher threshold than initial custody determinations to promote stability. In Texas, modification within one year of the order requires an additional showing of serious and immediate danger to the child's welfare.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. THRESHOLD: Has there been a material and substantial change in circumstances? 2. TIMING: Was prior order entered more or less than one year ago? Different standards may apply. 3. BEST INTEREST: Even if threshold met, modification must serve child's best interest. 4. SPECIFIC GROUNDS: Relocation, abuse, neglect, child's preference (if age-appropriate), parental incapacity. 5. STABILITY PREFERENCE: Courts disfavor frequent modification absent compelling grounds.
key_factors: Nature and degree of changed circumstances
Whether change was foreseeable at time of prior order
Any history of frivolous modification attempts

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Burgess, 13 Cal.4th 25 (1996)

counter_arguments: Material change standard is vague giving courts wide discretion
Stability preference may trap children in suboptimal arrangements
One-year restriction may not protect children in urgent situations
Foregone circumstances doctrine is inconsistently applied

blocks.conclusion_template: Relocation cases require balancing the relocating parent's right to mobility against the child's interest in maintaining meaningful contact with both parents. Most jurisdictions require notice to the non-relocating parent (30-60 days typical), and the relocating parent bears the burden of showing relocation serves the child's best interest. Courts consider the reason for the move, impact on visitation, quality of proposed substitute visitation schedule, and the child's ties to the current community.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. NOTICE REQUIREMENT: Was proper statutory notice given? 2. BURDEN: Relocating parent must show good faith and best interest (varies by state). 3. FACTORS: Reason for move, enhanced quality of life, feasibility of preserving other parent's relationship, child's preference, impact on child's development. 4. GEOGRAPHIC RESTRICTIONS: If existing order contains restriction, modification is required before relocation. 5. REMEDY: Court may modify custody, modify visitation, or deny relocation.
key_factors: Impact on child's relationship with non-relocating parent
Child's ties to current community and school
Quality of life enhancement for child

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Burgess, 13 Cal.4th 25 (1996)

primary_authority.relevance: Case-by-case best interest analysis for relocation (NY)

counter_arguments: Presumptions favoring custodial parent's relocation may undervalue other parent's relationship
Geographic restrictions limit parent's economic mobility
Best interest balancing is inherently speculative
Virtual visitation is inadequate substitute for in-person contact

blocks.conclusion_template: Family violence creates a rebuttable presumption against awarding custody (sole or joint) to the perpetrator in most jurisdictions. Courts must make specific findings regarding the impact of violence on the child's best interest. History of violence, protective orders, criminal convictions, completion of batterer intervention programs, and risk of future violence are all considered. The protective parent's credibility is enhanced, not diminished, by seeking protection.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. EVIDENCE OF VIOLENCE: Protective orders, criminal records, testimony, medical records, police reports. 2. PRESUMPTION: In states with statutory presumption, burden shifts to perpetrator to overcome. 3. IMPACT ON CHILD: Direct abuse, witnessing violence, climate of fear. 4. RISK ASSESSMENT: Likelihood of future violence, lethality indicators. 5. REMEDIAL MEASURES: BIP completion, sobriety, counseling, supervised visitation. 6. SAFETY PLANNING: Provisions for safe exchange, no-contact provisions, supervised access.
key_factors: Existence of protective orders or criminal convictions
Whether child witnessed or was victim of violence
Impact on child's emotional and physical safety
Whether violence was isolated or pattern

primary_authority.relevance: History of family violence considered in custody
Rebuttable presumption against custody for DV perpetrator
DV must be considered in best interest analysis

counter_arguments: False allegations of DV are used tactically in custody disputes
Presumptions may deny due process to accused parent
Isolated incident should not determine custody
Perpetrator rehabilitation should be given weight

blocks.conclusion_template: Courts impute income to a parent who is voluntarily unemployed or underemployed for purposes of child support and spousal support calculations. Income is imputed based on earning capacity considering education, work history, job market conditions, age, health, and any legitimate reason for reduced employment (e.g., caring for a young child). The burden is on the party seeking imputation to demonstrate voluntary underemployment; the responding party may rebut by showing good faith job search efforts or legitimate barriers to employment.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. VOLUNTARY ANALYSIS: Is the unemployment or underemployment voluntary? Layoff vs quitting. 2. GOOD FAITH: Has the parent made good faith efforts to find employment? 3. EARNING CAPACITY: Education, skills, work history, job market. 4. LEGITIMATE REASONS: Caring for young child, disability, retraining. 5. IMPUTATION AMOUNT: Based on actual earning capacity, not hypothetical maximum. 6. EVIDENCE: Pay stubs, tax returns, vocational expert testimony, job search records.

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Barth, 210 Ill.2d 97 (2004)

primary_authority.relevance: Earning capacity may be considered for support

counter_arguments: Imputation based on historical income may not reflect current market
Stay-at-home parent cannot easily re-enter workforce
Disability claims may be difficult to evaluate
Imputed income is inherently speculative

blocks.conclusion_template: Closely held businesses in divorce require formal valuation using accepted methodologies: income approach (capitalization of earnings, discounted cash flow), market approach (comparable transactions, guideline companies), and asset approach (adjusted net asset value). Courts must determine whether personal goodwill (non-marital in most states) can be separated from enterprise goodwill (marital). Valuation date, discount for lack of marketability, and minority interest discounts are frequently contested.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. CHARACTERIZATION: Is business community/marital or separate? When was it acquired/founded? 2. VALUATION DATE: Date of separation, filing, or trial depending on jurisdiction. 3. METHODOLOGY: Income, market, and/or asset approach. Expert testimony typically required. 4. GOODWILL SEPARATION: Personal goodwill (tied to individual) vs enterprise goodwill (business systems). 5. DISCOUNTS: Lack of marketability (DLOM), minority interest, key person. 6. FORENSIC ANALYSIS: Owner compensation normalization, personal expenses through business, hidden income.

primary_authority.relevance: Professional goodwill not divisible in TX divorce

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Brown, 15 Cal.3d 838 (1976)
primary_authority.relevance: Goodwill of professional practice is community property in CA

counter_arguments: Personal vs enterprise goodwill distinction is artificial
Valuation is inherently uncertain for closely held businesses
Discounts are subjective and expert-dependent
Historical earnings may not predict future performance

blocks.topic: Hidden Assets and Discovery in Divorce
blocks.conclusion_template: Concealment of assets in divorce proceedings constitutes fraud on the court and the other spouse. Discovery tools include interrogatories, requests for production, subpoenas to financial institutions, forensic accounting, lifestyle analysis, and depositions. Red flags include unexplained cash withdrawals, transfers to third parties, sudden business decline, cryptocurrency holdings, offshore accounts, and overpayment of taxes or creditors. Courts may impose sanctions including adverse inference, attorney fee awards, and disproportionate division favoring the non-concealing spouse.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. RED FLAG IDENTIFICATION: Cash lifestyle, unexplained transfers, business irregularities. 2. FORMAL DISCOVERY: Interrogatories, document requests, subpoenas. 3. FORENSIC ANALYSIS: Bank records, tax returns, business records, lifestyle analysis. 4. DIGITAL ASSETS: Cryptocurrency, NFTs, digital accounts, app-based financial services. 5. THIRD PARTY TRANSFERS: Transfers to family, friends, entities controlled by spouse. 6. SANCTIONS: Adverse inference, fee shifting, disproportionate division.
key_factors: Unexplained cash withdrawals or spending patterns
Transfers to related parties near divorce filing
Discrepancies between lifestyle and reported income

primary_authority.relevance: Fraud on the community — reconstitution of estate
Constructive fraud in community property division

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Rossi, 90 Cal.App.4th 34 (2001)
primary_authority.relevance: Entire hidden asset awarded to non-concealing spouse

counter_arguments: Discovery costs may exceed value of hidden assets
Forensic accounting is expensive and time-consuming
Cryptocurrency tracing is technically challenging
Offshore investigation requires international cooperation

blocks.conclusion_template: Dissipation occurs when one spouse uses marital assets for a non-marital purpose during the breakdown of the marriage, typically after the parties have separated or divorce is contemplated. The party alleging dissipation bears the initial burden of showing prima facie dissipation; the burden then shifts to the spending spouse to account for the expenditures. Courts may credit the non-dissipating spouse with the dissipated amount in the property division.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. TIMING: Did spending occur during marriage breakdown (post-separation or when divorce contemplated)? 2. PURPOSE: Was spending for a non-marital purpose (affair expenses, gambling, substance abuse, gifts to paramour)? 3. AMOUNT: Is the amount material relative to the marital estate? 4. ACCOUNTING: Can the spending spouse account for and justify the expenditures? 5. REMEDY: Credit dissipated amount to non-dissipating spouse in division.
key_factors: Whether funds used for non-marital purpose
Amount relative to total marital estate
Whether spending spouse can account for funds

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of O'Neill, 138 Ill.2d 487 (1990)

primary_authority.relevance: Illinois dissipation factor in property division
Dissipation requires intentional waste during breakdown

counter_arguments: Normal living expenses during separation are not dissipation
Spending on children benefits the community
Business losses are not intentional dissipation
Timing of breakdown is often disputed

blocks.topic: Modification of Child or Spousal Support
blocks.conclusion_template: Modification of child or spousal support requires a showing of material and substantial change in circumstances since the prior order. Common grounds include significant income change (increase or decrease), job loss, disability, retirement, remarriage of recipient (spousal support), changed needs of child, or emancipation of child. The movant bears the burden of proving both the changed circumstance and that modification is warranted. Voluntary changes in income are scrutinized for good faith.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. CHANGED CIRCUMSTANCE: Identify what has materially changed since the prior order. 2. INVOLUNTARY vs VOLUNTARY: Was the change within the obligor's control? 3. DURATION: Is the change temporary or permanent? 4. RECALCULATION: Apply current guidelines to current incomes. 5. RETROACTIVITY: Modification typically effective from date of filing, not earlier. 6. PROCEDURAL: File motion, serve other party, hearing required.
key_factors: Nature and degree of income change
Whether change is voluntary or involuntary
Good faith of party seeking reduction
Current needs of child or spouse

primary_authority.relevance: Modification of child support on material change
Changed circumstances standard for support modification

counter_arguments: Voluntary income reduction should not reduce support obligation
Job loss may be temporary and not warrant modification
Obligor may manipulate income through entity structuring
Retroactivity limitation may create hardship

blocks.conclusion_template: Parental alienation refers to a pattern of behavior by one parent intended to damage the child's relationship with the other parent. Courts recognize alienating behavior as a factor in custody determinations, though 'Parental Alienation Syndrome' (PAS) as a clinical diagnosis remains controversial and is not accepted by the APA. Evidence of alienation includes disparaging the other parent to the child, interfering with communication or visitation, making false allegations, and coaching the child to reject the other parent. Severe alienation may result in custody change to the alienated parent.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. BEHAVIORAL EVIDENCE: Identify specific alienating behaviors (disparagement, interference, coaching, false allegations). 2. CHILD RESPONSE: Does the child exhibit rejection disproportionate to any legitimate grievance? 3. DISTINGUISH FROM ESTRANGEMENT: Genuine estrangement based on the child's own experience with a parent is not alienation. 4. SEVERITY: Mild (occasional disparagement) vs severe (complete rejection without basis). 5. REMEDY: Reunification therapy, custody modification, sanctions, contempt.
key_factors: Pattern of disparaging other parent to child
Whether behaviors constitute estrangement vs alienation

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Bates, 212 Ill.2d 489 (2004)
primary_authority.relevance: Alienating behavior as custody modification ground
False child abuse allegations as factor in custody

primary_authority.reference: Karen B. v. Clyde M., 151 A.D.3d 1 (N.Y. App. 2017)
primary_authority.relevance: Custody reversal based on severe alienation
PAS not recognized as clinical diagnosis

counter_arguments: Alienation claims may mask legitimate protective concerns
PAS is not scientifically validated
Children may have genuine reasons for rejecting a parent
Forced reunification can be harmful if abuse occurred

blocks.conclusion_template: The Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (UCCJEA), adopted in all 50 states and DC, establishes jurisdictional priority for custody matters. Home state jurisdiction (state where child lived for 6 consecutive months prior to filing) has priority. Once a state exercises jurisdiction, it retains exclusive continuing jurisdiction until the child and all parties leave the state or the court declines jurisdiction. Emergency jurisdiction exists for abuse/neglect situations but is temporary.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. HOME STATE: Where did child live for 6 months before filing? This state has priority. 2. SIGNIFICANT CONNECTION: If no home state, state with significant connection and substantial evidence. 3. EXCLUSIVE CONTINUING: If prior order exists, original state retains jurisdiction. 4. EMERGENCY: Temporary emergency jurisdiction for abuse/neglect/abandonment. 5. INCONVENIENT FORUM: Court may decline jurisdiction in favor of more appropriate state. 6. SIMULTANEOUS PROCEEDINGS: Courts must communicate and resolve conflicting proceedings.
key_factors: Child's home state for 6 months prior to filing
Whether another state has concurrent proceedings
counter_arguments: Home state determination is disputed when family moves frequently
Emergency jurisdiction scope is vague
Continuing jurisdiction may persist even when inconvenient
International cases add Hague Convention complexity

blocks.conclusion_template: Paternity may be established by presumption (marriage to mother at birth), voluntary acknowledgment, adjudication, or genetic testing. The marital presumption is rebuttable but requires clear and convincing evidence in most jurisdictions. Voluntary acknowledgment has the force of a court order after the statutory rescission period (typically 60 days). Genetic testing is conclusive at 99% or greater probability of paternity. Establishing paternity creates rights and obligations including custody, visitation, support, and inheritance.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. PRESUMPTION: Is there a marital presumption? Was the mother married at conception or birth? 2. ACKNOWLEDGMENT: Was a voluntary acknowledgment of paternity executed? Has rescission period passed? 3. GENETIC TESTING: Has DNA testing been ordered or completed? 4. STANDING: Who has standing to challenge or establish paternity? 5. TIMELINESS: Statute of limitations for paternity actions varies by state. 6. CONSEQUENCES: Support obligation, custody rights, inheritance rights.
key_factors: Best interest of child in challenging paternity
Reliance interests of child and parties

primary_authority.reference: Michael H. v. Gerald D., 491 U.S. 110 (1989)

primary_authority.relevance: Federal requirements for state paternity proceedings

counter_arguments: Marital presumption may not reflect biological reality
Acknowledging paternity without DNA testing is risky
Challenging established paternity may harm child's reliance interests
Standing restrictions may bar biological father from establishing rights

blocks.conclusion_template: Protective orders in family law provide injunctive relief against family violence, stalking, or harassment. Temporary ex parte orders (TROs) may be granted without notice to the respondent upon a showing of immediate danger. Permanent protective orders (typically 1-2 years, renewable) require notice and hearing. Violation of a protective order is a criminal offense in all jurisdictions. Orders typically prohibit contact, require distance, may award temporary custody and support, and order surrender of firearms.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. GROUNDS: Family violence, sexual assault, stalking, or harassment. 2. EX PARTE TRO: Immediate and present danger of family violence. 3. HEARING: Within 14-20 days for permanent order. 4. EVIDENCE: Testimony, police reports, medical records, photographs, text messages. 5. PROVISIONS: No contact, stay away distance, temporary custody, firearms surrender. 6. ENFORCEMENT: Criminal prosecution for violation, contempt.
key_factors: Evidence of family violence or threat

primary_authority.relevance: Full faith and credit for protective orders

primary_authority.reference: Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales, 545 U.S. 748 (2005)
primary_authority.relevance: No constitutional right to police enforcement of PO

counter_arguments: Ex parte orders may be granted without adequate due process
Protective orders may be sought for tactical advantage in custody
Enforcement depends on police discretion
Firearms provisions may conflict with Second Amendment claims

blocks.topic: Enforcement and Contempt of Court Orders
blocks.conclusion_template: Contempt is the primary enforcement mechanism for family court orders. Civil (coercive) contempt aims to compel compliance and the contemnor holds the keys to their release. Criminal contempt punishes past violations with due process protections including right to counsel and proof beyond reasonable doubt. The movant must prove: (1) a clear and specific order existed, (2) the respondent had knowledge of the order, (3) the respondent had the ability to comply, and (4) the respondent willfully failed to comply. Inability to comply is an affirmative defense.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. ORDER: Is the order clear, specific, and unambiguous? 2. KNOWLEDGE: Did respondent have actual or constructive knowledge? 3. VIOLATION: What specific provision was violated and how? 4. WILLFULNESS: Was the violation intentional, not merely negligent? 5. ABILITY: Did respondent have the ability to comply? 6. REMEDY: Civil (coercive jail, fines until compliance) or criminal (punishment for past violation). 7. PURGE CONDITIONS: What must respondent do to purge the contempt?
key_factors: Clarity of the order allegedly violated
Impact on children or other party

primary_authority.relevance: Right to counsel in civil contempt for child support

counter_arguments: Ability to pay is often disputed in support contempt
Incarcerating indigent obligors does not generate support payments
Civil vs criminal contempt distinction is blurred in practice
Contempt may be disproportionate remedy for minor violations

blocks.conclusion_template: Property owned before marriage, acquired by gift or inheritance during marriage, or representing personal injury recovery (pain and suffering component) is separate property. The party claiming separate character bears the burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence. When separate and community funds are commingled, tracing is required using either the community-out-first method or the minimum sum balance method. Failure to trace results in community characterization.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. INCEPTION OF TITLE: When was the property first acquired? Before marriage = separate. 2. SOURCE OF FUNDS: Gift, inheritance, or pre-marital source documented? 3. COMMINGLING: Were separate funds mixed with community funds? 4. TRACING: Can the separate character be traced through the commingled account? 5. METHOD: Community-out-first or minimum sum balance. 6. MUTATION: Has separate property been transmuted by agreement or gift?
key_factors: Date of acquisition relative to marriage

primary_authority.relevance: Texas separate and community property definitions
Clear and convincing standard for separate property

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Mix, 14 Cal.3d 604 (1975)

counter_arguments: Tracing decades-old transactions is often impossible
Community-out-first method can be manipulated
Improvements to separate property using community funds create reimbursement claims
Separate property income may be community in some states

blocks.conclusion_template: Division of retirement benefits in divorce requires a Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) for ERISA-governed plans (401k, pension, profit sharing). The QDRO must be approved by both the court and the plan administrator. Division methods include immediate offset (one spouse receives other assets of equivalent value) or deferred distribution (benefits divided at retirement). The coverture fraction (years of marriage during participation / total years of participation) determines the marital portion. IRAs are divided by transfer incident to divorce under IRC 408(d)(6) without a QDRO.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. PLAN TYPE: ERISA qualified plan (needs QDRO) or IRA (transfer incident to divorce)? 2. COVERTURE FRACTION: Marital portion = marriage overlap with plan participation. 3. DIVISION METHOD: Immediate offset vs deferred distribution. 4. DRAFTING: QDRO must comply with plan requirements and ERISA. 5. APPROVAL: Submit to plan administrator for pre-approval, then court order. 6. TAX: Transfer under QDRO is not a taxable event; distribution to alternate payee is taxed to recipient.

primary_authority.relevance: State courts cannot divide military disability pay

counter_arguments: Immediate offset requires accurate present-value calculation
Deferred distribution creates ongoing entanglement between ex-spouses
Plan administrator rejection can delay division
Military and government pensions have unique rules

blocks.conclusion_template: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA) eliminated the alimony deduction for divorce agreements executed after December 31, 2018. Property transfers incident to divorce are tax-free under IRC 1041 but carry over the transferor's basis. Filing status is determined by marital status on December 31. Child-related tax benefits (Child Tax Credit, Head of Household status) are allocated to the custodial parent unless Form 8332 releases the claim. Capital gains exclusion under IRC 121 may be affected by divorce timing.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. ALIMONY: Pre-2019 agreements: deductible/includable. Post-2018: no tax consequence. 2. PROPERTY TRANSFERS: IRC 1041 nonrecognition, basis carryover. 3. FILING STATUS: Married or single as of Dec 31; Head of Household requires maintaining household for dependent. 4. CHILD TAX BENEFITS: CTC, EITC, HOH status follow custodial parent unless released. 5. RESIDENCE: IRC 121 exclusion ($250K/$500K) — timing of sale relative to divorce. 6. RETIREMENT: QDRO transfers are not taxable events.
key_factors: Date of divorce agreement (pre/post 2019 for alimony)

primary_authority.relevance: Nonrecognition on transfers between spouses/incident to divorce
Capital gains exclusion on sale of principal residence

counter_arguments: TCJA alimony change shifts tax burden unfavorably in many cases
Basis carryover on appreciated assets creates deferred tax liability
Filing status planning depends on divorce timing which may not be controllable
Complex tax rules are often overlooked in settlement negotiations

blocks.conclusion_template: Temporary orders maintain the status quo and protect parties and children during the pendency of divorce or custody proceedings. Courts may award temporary custody, temporary support (child and spousal), exclusive possession of the marital home, temporary restraining orders on assets, and interim attorney fees. The standard for temporary orders is lower than final orders — courts consider the immediate needs and circumstances rather than conducting full best-interest or equitable division analysis.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. IMMEDIATE NEEDS: What must be addressed before final trial? 2. STATUS QUO: Maintain existing arrangements to extent possible. 3. TEMPORARY CUSTODY: Immediate best interest, not full evaluation. 4. TEMPORARY SUPPORT: Based on current financial need and ability to pay. 5. ASSET PRESERVATION: Mutual restraining orders on dissipation, transfer, destruction. 6. DURATION: In effect until final order or further court order.
key_factors: Immediate needs of children and parties

primary_authority.relevance: Temporary orders in suit affecting parent-child relationship
Appellate review standard for temporary orders

counter_arguments: Temporary orders often become de facto permanent due to status quo bias
Lower standard may result in less thorough analysis
Temporary support may not reflect actual needs
Asset freezes may cause hardship to both parties

blocks.topic: Attorney Fee Awards in Family Law
blocks.conclusion_template: Family courts have broad discretion to award attorney fees to ensure equal access to the legal process. Courts consider the financial resources of each party, reasonableness of fees incurred, complexity of issues, and conduct of the parties. Interim fee awards ensure the less-resourced spouse can participate meaningfully. Fee awards may also serve as sanctions for discovery abuse, frivolous motions, or other bad faith conduct.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. NEED: Does requesting party lack resources for adequate representation? 2. ABILITY: Does other party have ability to pay? 3. REASONABLENESS: Are fees reasonable for the complexity and duration? 4. NECESSITY: Were the fees necessarily incurred? 5. CONDUCT: Did either party's conduct increase fees unnecessarily? 6. INTERIM vs FINAL: Interim fees to level the playing field; final fees in the decree.

primary_authority.relevance: Attorney fee awards in family cases
Need-based attorney fee awards in California

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Tharp, 131 Cal.App.4th 624 (2005)
primary_authority.relevance: Fee award to ensure parity of representation
NY attorney fee awards in matrimonial actions

counter_arguments: Fee awards are discretionary with limited appellate review
Reasonable fee determination is subjective
Interim fees may not be recovered if requesting party prevails
Fee-shifting may incentivize litigation rather than settlement

blocks.conclusion_template: Parenting plans allocate physical possession of children between parents on a regular schedule, holidays, summers, and special occasions. Most jurisdictions have a standard possession order (SPO) that applies as a default. Plans should address exchange logistics, communication protocols, decision-making authority, geographic restrictions, right of first refusal, and dispute resolution. Courts favor detailed, specific plans that minimize conflict and provide predictability for children.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. STANDARD vs CUSTOM: Does the standard possession order work for this family? 2. AGE-APPROPRIATE: Young children may need modified schedules. 3. LOGISTICS: Exchange locations, transportation, communication. 4. HOLIDAYS: Alternating, fixed, or divided schedule. 5. DECISION-MAKING: Joint vs sole on education, medical, religious, extracurricular. 6. FLEXIBILITY: Right of first refusal, makeup time, communication provisions.
key_factors: Age and developmental needs of children

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Brown & Yana, 37 Cal.4th 947 (2006)
primary_authority.relevance: Joint custody and parenting plan standards

counter_arguments: Standard possession orders may not fit every family
Young children may suffer from overnight separations
Rigid schedules limit flexibility for older children
Geographic restrictions conflict with parent's mobility rights

blocks.conclusion_template: Courts may deviate from guideline child support when strict application would be unjust or inappropriate. Common grounds include extraordinary medical expenses, educational needs, travel costs for long-distance possession, multiple family obligations, and income above or below the guideline range. Deviation must be supported by specific findings on the record. High-income cases often require deviation analysis because guideline tables cap at a specific income level.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. GUIDELINE CALCULATION: Start with guideline amount. 2. DEVIATION GROUNDS: Identify statutory basis for deviation. 3. EVIDENCE: Document why guidelines are unjust or inappropriate. 4. FINDINGS: Court must make specific findings supporting deviation. 5. BEST INTEREST: Deviation must still serve child's best interest.
key_factors: Whether guideline amount meets child's needs

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Bush, 191 Ill. App. 3d 249 (1989)

counter_arguments: Deviation undermines guideline predictability
Judicial discretion in deviation is hard to review on appeal
High-income deviation may result in windfall to custodial parent

blocks.conclusion_template: Retroactive child support may be ordered back to the date of the child's birth (paternity cases) or the date of separation/filing (divorce cases), subject to statutory limitations. Courts consider whether the obligor knew of the child's existence, whether the obligee sought support timely, the obligor's ability to pay retroactively, and the needs of the child during the retroactive period. In Texas, retroactive support is limited to four years before the date of filing.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. STATUTORY LIMIT: What is the maximum retroactive period? 2. KNOWLEDGE: Did the obligor know of paternity/obligation? 3. DELAY: Was there unreasonable delay in seeking support? 4. ABILITY: Did obligor have ability to pay during retroactive period? 5. NEEDS: Were the child's needs met during the period? 6. CALCULATION: Apply guidelines to historical income.
key_factors: Obligor's knowledge of child or obligation
Reason for delay in seeking support
Obligor's historical income and ability to pay
Obligor's access to child during period

primary_authority.relevance: Factors for retroactive support in paternity cases
Federal requirement for retroactive support enforcement

counter_arguments: Retroactive obligations may be financially devastating
Delayed paternity establishment should not penalize obligor
Historical income may be difficult to reconstruct
Laches should apply to unreasonable delay

blocks.conclusion_template: Military divorce involves unique federal considerations under the Uniformed Services Former Spouses' Protection Act (USFSPA). State courts may divide disposable retired pay as marital property. The 10/10 rule (10 years of marriage overlapping 10 years of service) enables direct payment from DFAS but does not limit the right to divide the pension. Disability pay cannot be divided. The Survivor Benefit Plan (SBP) requires election or court order. Jurisdiction requires the servicemember's domicile, residence, or consent.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. JURISDICTION: Is the court in the servicemember's domicile, residence, or consent state? 2. CHARACTERIZATION: Military retired pay is divisible marital property. 3. COVERTURE: Marital share = months married during service / total months of service. 4. 10/10 RULE: Only affects direct DFAS payment, not divisibility. 5. DISABILITY OFFSET: VA disability pay replaces retired pay and is not divisible. 6. SBP: Must be addressed to protect former spouse's interest.
key_factors: Length of marriage overlapping military service
Rank and years of service at retirement or divorce
Whether member has retired or divorce is pre-retirement

primary_authority.relevance: Authority for state courts to divide military retired pay
States cannot divide military disability pay even indirectly

counter_arguments: Disability offset creates windfall to servicemember at former spouse's expense
Pre-retirement division requires hypothetical calculation
SBP costs reduce net retired pay
Jurisdiction requirements may bar action in convenient forum

blocks.topic: Hague Convention on International Child Abduction
blocks.conclusion_template: The Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (implemented in the US by ICARA, 22 U.S.C. 9001-9011) provides for the prompt return of children wrongfully removed or retained across international borders. The petitioner must establish that the child was habitually resident in the requesting state and the removal violated custody rights under that state's law. Defenses include consent, grave risk of harm, child's objection (if of sufficient age), and fundamental rights violations. The Convention is a jurisdictional remedy, not a custody determination.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. HABITUAL RESIDENCE: Where was the child habitually resident before removal? 2. CUSTODY RIGHTS: Did the left-behind parent have custody rights under that state's law? 3. WRONGFUL REMOVAL: Was the removal in breach of those rights? 4. DEFENSES: Consent, acquiescence, grave risk, settled in new environment, child's objection. 5. TIMING: Petition within one year of wrongful removal for strongest claim. 6. RETURN: Remedy is return to habitual residence, not custody determination.
key_factors: Whether left-behind parent had custody rights
Grave risk of harm to child
Child's age and maturity for objection defense

primary_authority.relevance: Equitable tolling not available for one-year period

counter_arguments: Habitual residence test is fact-intensive and unpredictable
Grave risk defense is narrowly construed
Return to abusive home environment may be ordered
Convention does not apply to non-signatory countries

blocks.topic: De Facto Parent / Psychological Parent Doctrine
blocks.conclusion_template: The de facto parent doctrine grants standing and potential custody or visitation rights to non-biological, non-adoptive individuals who have functioned as a parent with the legal parent's consent. Requirements typically include: living with the child for a significant period, assuming parental obligations, establishing a bonded relationship, and the legal parent having fostered or supported the relationship. Recognition varies significantly by jurisdiction. Some states have statutory frameworks; others rely on common law.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. STANDING: Does the claimant meet de facto parent criteria under applicable law? 2. CONSENT: Did the legal parent encourage or consent to the parental relationship? 3. DURATION: How long and how consistently did the claimant function as a parent? 4. BOND: Is there a significant parent-child bond? 5. BEST INTEREST: Even if standing is established, custody/visitation must serve the child's best interest. 6. PARENTAL PRESUMPTION: The legal parent's rights are presumptively superior to any third party.
key_factors: Whether legal parent consented to relationship
Nature and extent of parental responsibilities assumed
Impact on child of severing relationship

primary_authority.reference: In re Custody of H.S.H.-K., 193 Wis.2d 649 (1995)

primary_authority.relevance: Parental rights presumption against third-party visitation

counter_arguments: De facto parent doctrine may infringe on legal parent's constitutional rights
Duration and consent requirements are vague
May open door to unwanted custody claims by former partners
Inconsistent recognition across states creates forum shopping

blocks.conclusion_template: Grandparent visitation rights are limited by the constitutional presumption that fit parents act in their children's best interest (Troxel v. Granville). Most states permit grandparent visitation petitions only in specific circumstances: when the nuclear family has been disrupted (divorce, death of a parent, parental incarceration), when the child previously lived with the grandparent, or when denial would cause significant harm. The grandparent bears the burden of overcoming the parental presumption, typically requiring clear and convincing evidence.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. STANDING: Does the grandparent meet statutory standing requirements? 2. PARENTAL FITNESS: Is the parent fit? If so, strong presumption in parent's favor. 3. SIGNIFICANT HARM: Would denial of visitation cause significant harm to the child? 4. BEST INTEREST: Would visitation serve the child's best interest? 5. SPECIAL CIRCUMSTANCES: Death of parent, divorce, prior custodial relationship. 6. CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITS: Troxel requires special weight to fit parent's wishes.
key_factors: Prior relationship between grandparent and child
Whether nuclear family has been disrupted
Evidence of significant harm from denial
Parent's stated reasons for denying visitation

primary_authority.relevance: Due process limits on third-party visitation
Presumption in favor of fit parent

counter_arguments: Grandparent visitation statutes may be unconstitutional as applied
Significant harm standard is too restrictive
Parent's animus toward grandparent should not deny child relationship
Special weight to parental wishes makes relief nearly impossible

blocks.conclusion_template: Emancipation grants a minor legal adult status for specified purposes, typically including contracting, consenting to medical treatment, establishing residence, and managing earnings. Requirements vary by jurisdiction but generally include: minimum age (typically 16-17), self-sufficiency demonstrated by employment and separate residence, and a showing that emancipation serves the minor's best interest. Emancipation terminates child support obligations and parental authority. Courts may grant full or partial emancipation.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. AGE: Does the minor meet minimum age requirement? 2. SELF-SUFFICIENCY: Can the minor support themselves financially? 3. MATURITY: Does the minor demonstrate sufficient maturity? 4. BEST INTEREST: Is emancipation in the minor's best interest? 5. PARENTAL CONSENT: Is parental consent required or available? 6. SCOPE: Full emancipation vs removal of specific disabilities.

primary_authority.relevance: Texas removal of disabilities of minority

primary_authority.reference: In re Anonymous, 150 Misc.2d 67 (N.Y. Fam. Ct. 1991)

counter_arguments: Self-sufficiency at 16-17 is difficult to maintain
Emancipation terminates safety net of parental support
Minor may lack maturity to understand long-term consequences
Partial emancipation creates uncertain legal status

blocks.conclusion_template: Annulment declares a marriage void or voidable ab initio, as if it never existed, unlike divorce which dissolves a valid marriage. Void marriages (bigamy, incest, underage without consent) are invalid from inception and need no court action. Voidable marriages (fraud, duress, mental incapacity, impotence, intoxication) are valid until annulled by court order. Property and support rights after annulment vary by jurisdiction — some states apply equitable division principles, others treat parties as unmarried. Children of annulled marriages retain legitimacy.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. VOID vs VOIDABLE: Was the marriage void from inception or voidable? 2. GROUNDS: Identify specific statutory ground for annulment. 3. TIMELINESS: Was annulment sought within statutory time limit? 4. RATIFICATION: Did the complaining party ratify the marriage after the impediment was removed? 5. PROPERTY: How will property be divided — community/equitable or as unmarried persons? 6. CHILDREN: Children remain legitimate regardless of annulment.
key_factors: Whether marriage is void or voidable
Whether impediment was removed and marriage ratified

primary_authority.relevance: California void and voidable marriage grounds
Putative spouse doctrine for property after annulment

counter_arguments: Annulment may deprive spouse of community/marital property rights
Statute of limitations may bar annulment
Ratification may waive right to annulment
Putative spouse doctrine is inconsistently applied

blocks.conclusion_template: Legal separation provides court-ordered division of rights and responsibilities without dissolving the marriage. Not all states recognize legal separation (Texas does not). Where available, it addresses property division, support, custody, and debt allocation while maintaining marital status. Reasons for choosing separation over divorce include religious objections, health insurance continuation, tax benefits, and potential reconciliation. Separation agreements are enforceable contracts and may be incorporated into a later divorce decree.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. AVAILABILITY: Does the jurisdiction recognize legal separation? 2. GROUNDS: Are grounds required (same as divorce) or no-fault? 3. SCOPE: Property, support, custody — all addressable. 4. CONVERSION: Can separation be converted to divorce? 5. INSURANCE: Does separation preserve health insurance benefits? 6. ENFORCEABILITY: Separation agreements are binding contracts.
key_factors: Reason for choosing separation over divorce
Impact on health insurance and benefits
counter_arguments: Legal separation creates ongoing legal entanglement
Neither party can remarry
Property and financial changes during separation create complications
Some states do not recognize legal separation

blocks.conclusion_template: Common law (informal) marriage is recognized in a minority of states (TX, CO, UT, IA, KS, MT, SC, NH, DC, and others by prior recognition). In Texas, elements are: (1) agreement to be married, (2) cohabitation in Texas, and (3) holding out to the public as married. No ceremony or license is required. Once established, a common law marriage has the same legal effect as a ceremonial marriage. The party asserting common law marriage bears the burden of proof.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. JURISDICTION: Does the state recognize common law marriage? 2. ELEMENTS: Agreement + cohabitation + holding out (TX). Vary by state. 3. EVIDENCE: Joint tax returns, shared surname, joint accounts, testimony of friends/family. 4. EFFECT: Same as ceremonial marriage — requires divorce to dissolve. 5. CONFLICT OF LAWS: Marriage valid where contracted is generally valid everywhere. 6. BURDEN: On party asserting the marriage.
key_factors: Whether jurisdiction recognizes common law marriage
Evidence of agreement to be married
How parties held themselves out to public

primary_authority.relevance: Evidence required for common law marriage in Texas

primary_authority.reference: In re Estate of Claveria, 615 S.W.2d 164 (Tex. 1981)

counter_arguments: Evidence of agreement is often disputed and circumstantial
Cohabitation alone does not create marriage
Holding out requirement is subjective
Party may dispute marriage to avoid property division

blocks.conclusion_template: Following Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), same-sex marriages are subject to the same divorce laws as opposite-sex marriages in all jurisdictions. Unique issues include: determination of marital duration (from date of ceremonial marriage, civil union, or domestic partnership), pre-Obergefell property characterization, parental rights for non-biological parents, and recognition of out-of-state marriages or civil unions. Courts apply standard divorce principles but may face novel fact patterns regarding parentage and property acquired before marriage was legally recognized.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. MARRIAGE DATE: When was the marriage or civil union established? 2. PROPERTY: Was property acquired before or after marriage was legal in the jurisdiction? 3. PARENTAGE: Were children born through ART, surrogacy, or adoption? 4. NON-BIO PARENT: Does the non-biological parent have legal parentage? 5. STANDARD DIVORCE: Apply same community property/equitable distribution rules.
key_factors: Date of marriage or civil union

primary_authority.relevance: Parentage for children of assisted reproduction
Full faith and credit for same-sex adoption

counter_arguments: Pre-Obergefell cohabitation period creates property characterization uncertainty
Non-biological parent may lack legal parentage if adoption not completed
Some jurisdictions slow to adapt procedures
Civil union vs marriage distinction may persist for some benefits

blocks.conclusion_template: Surrogacy law varies dramatically by jurisdiction. Gestational surrogacy (surrogate has no genetic relationship to child) is more widely recognized than traditional surrogacy (surrogate provides egg). Pre-birth parentage orders are available in many states, establishing intended parents as legal parents before birth. Enforceable surrogacy agreements typically require: independent counsel for all parties, medical/psychological screening, compensation terms, and compliance with state statutory requirements. Some states (MI, NY pre-2021) ban compensated surrogacy; others have comprehensive frameworks.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. TYPE: Gestational vs traditional surrogacy — different legal frameworks. 2. JURISDICTION: What does the state allow? 3. AGREEMENT: Does the agreement meet statutory requirements? 4. PARENTAGE ORDER: Can a pre-birth order be obtained? 5. CONFLICT: If surrogate refuses to relinquish, what is the remedy? 6. INTERSTATE/INTERNATIONAL: Conflict of laws for cross-border surrogacy.
key_factors: Whether pre-birth parentage order is available
Genetic relationship of intended parents to child
counter_arguments: Surrogacy commercializes reproduction
Traditional surrogacy agreements are unenforceable in many states
International surrogacy creates citizenship complications
Conflict when surrogate changes mind is legally complex

blocks.conclusion_template: Stepparent adoption terminates the legal rights and obligations of the non-custodial biological parent and creates a new parent-child relationship with the stepparent. Requirements include: consent of the biological parent (or termination of their rights), consent of the child if over a certain age, and a finding that adoption serves the child's best interest. Consent may be dispensed with if the biological parent has abandoned the child, failed to support the child for a statutory period, or had parental rights terminated. Home study requirements may be waived for stepparents.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. CONSENT: Has the biological parent consented or can consent be dispensed with? 2. GROUNDS TO DISPENSE: Abandonment, failure to support, termination of rights. 3. BEST INTEREST: Does adoption serve the child's best interest? 4. HOME STUDY: Is one required for stepparents? Usually waived. 5. EFFECT: Terminates all rights/obligations of biological parent. 6. CHILD CONSENT: Required if child is over statutory age (typically 12).
key_factors: Child's wishes if of sufficient age
Whether biological parent has maintained relationship

primary_authority.relevance: Grounds for termination of parental rights
Clear and convincing standard for termination and adoption

counter_arguments: Biological parent may contest consent dispensation
Termination of parental rights is disfavored and heavily scrutinized
Child may have conflicting feelings about adoption
Failure to support alone may not justify dispensing with consent

blocks.conclusion_template: Involuntary termination of parental rights (TPR) is the most severe family law remedy, requiring clear and convincing evidence of statutory grounds AND that termination is in the child's best interest. The constitutional right to parent means TPR requires heightened due process protections. Grounds include: abandonment, severe neglect or abuse, failure to support, conviction of certain crimes, failure to comply with service plan, mental illness rendering parent unable to care for child, and endangerment. TPR is a prerequisite for adoption without consent.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. GROUNDS: Identify specific statutory ground(s) for termination. 2. BURDEN: Clear and convincing evidence required (Santosky v. Kramer). 3. BEST INTEREST: Even if grounds proven, must still serve child's best interest. 4. DUE PROCESS: Right to counsel in most states, adequate notice, meaningful hearing. 5. ALTERNATIVES: Court should consider alternatives less drastic than termination. 6. EFFECT: Permanent — severs all legal ties between parent and child.
key_factors: Quality of evidence meeting clear and convincing standard

primary_authority.relevance: Clear and convincing evidence required for TPR
Factual sufficiency review for TPR findings
Federal ASFA requirements for TPR timelines

counter_arguments: TPR is irreversible and constitutional right is at stake
Parent may be able to remedy conditions with more time
Child may prefer maintaining parental relationship
Racial and economic bias in TPR proceedings is documented

blocks.conclusion_template: Supervised visitation is ordered when unsupervised contact poses a risk to the child's physical or emotional safety. Grounds include: history of abuse or neglect, substance abuse, mental health concerns, domestic violence, parental alienation, or lack of established relationship. Supervision may be by a professional provider, family member, or friend approved by the court. Courts should include specific terms regarding location, duration, supervisor qualifications, and conditions for transition to unsupervised access.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. RISK ASSESSMENT: What specific risk does unsupervised contact pose? 2. LEVEL: Professional supervision, family member, or therapeutic supervision. 3. CONDITIONS: Location, frequency, duration, approved activities. 4. TRANSITION PLAN: What must parent demonstrate to earn unsupervised access? 5. COST: Who bears cost of professional supervision? 6. REVIEW: Periodic review and modification based on progress.
key_factors: Nature and severity of concern prompting supervision
Parent's progress in addressing underlying issues
Plan for transitioning to unsupervised access

primary_authority.relevance: Supervised visitation for family violence history

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Battenburg, 28 Cal.App.4th 1338 (1994)

counter_arguments: Supervised visitation may not adequately protect child in severe cases
Professional supervision is expensive
Family member supervisors may not be impartial
Indefinite supervision may effectively terminate relationship

blocks.topic: Guardian ad Litem and Amicus Attorney
blocks.conclusion_template: A guardian ad litem (GAL) is appointed by the court to represent the child's best interest in custody proceedings. The GAL investigates facts, interviews parties and children, reviews records, and makes recommendations to the court. An amicus attorney represents the child's expressed wishes rather than the GAL's determination of best interest. CASA (Court Appointed Special Advocates) serve a similar function in dependency cases. The GAL's recommendations are advisory; the court makes the final determination.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. APPOINTMENT: When is a GAL mandatory vs discretionary? 2. ROLE: Best interest advocate (GAL) vs expressed wishes (amicus). 3. INVESTIGATION: What should the GAL investigate? 4. REPORT: Written report and recommendations to the court. 5. TESTIMONY: Can the GAL testify? (Varies by jurisdiction). 6. CONFIDENTIALITY: Scope of privilege and reporting obligations.
key_factors: Whether appointment is mandatory or discretionary

primary_authority.relevance: Texas GAL and amicus attorney provisions
Federal CAPTA requirement for GAL in abuse/neglect cases
GAL duties and standards in Texas

primary_authority.reference: NACC Recommendations for Representation of Children

counter_arguments: GAL recommendations are not binding but carry significant weight
GAL investigation quality varies widely
Cost of GAL may be prohibitive for some families
GAL may substitute personal values for legal analysis

blocks.conclusion_template: Most jurisdictions require mediation before trial in family law cases. Mediation is confidential, voluntary in outcome (parties cannot be forced to settle), and conducted by a neutral mediator. Exceptions to mandatory mediation include cases involving family violence, where mediation may re-traumatize the victim or create power imbalance. Mediated settlement agreements are binding contracts enforceable as court orders. Mediator testimony and communications are privileged and inadmissible.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. REQUIREMENT: Is mediation mandatory in this jurisdiction/case? 2. EXCEPTION: Does a domestic violence exception apply? 3. SELECTION: Court-appointed or party-selected mediator? 4. CONFIDENTIALITY: All communications privileged and inadmissible. 5. AGREEMENT: If reached, binding contract enforceable as order. 6. IMPASSE: If no agreement, case proceeds to trial.

primary_authority.relevance: Texas mediation provisions in family cases

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Kieturakis, 138 Cal.App.4th 56 (2006)

counter_arguments: Mediation may perpetuate power imbalances
DV exception is underutilized
Mediators lack authority to compel disclosure
Rushed mediation may result in unfair agreements

blocks.conclusion_template: Collaborative divorce is a voluntary, non-adversarial process where both parties and their attorneys commit to resolving all issues without court intervention. The hallmark is the disqualification provision: if the process fails, both attorneys must withdraw and parties must retain new counsel for litigation. The process typically involves a team including attorneys, financial professionals, and mental health coaches. Collaborative agreements are enforceable contracts. The process is not suitable for cases involving domestic violence, hidden assets, or extreme power imbalances.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. PARTICIPATION AGREEMENT: Both parties and attorneys sign commitment to collaborative process. 2. DISQUALIFICATION: Attorneys cannot represent in litigation if process fails. 3. TEAM: Financial neutral, child specialist, communication coaches. 4. DISCLOSURE: Full voluntary disclosure required — no formal discovery. 5. AGREEMENT: Result is binding settlement agreement. 6. SUITABILITY: Screen for DV, power imbalance, and hidden assets.
key_factors: Whether both parties voluntarily agree to process

primary_authority.relevance: Model statutory framework for collaborative law

primary_authority.reference: IACP Ethical Standards for Collaborative Practitioners

counter_arguments: Disqualification provision creates perverse incentive to settle at any cost
Power imbalances may not be apparent until process is underway
No formal discovery means potential for incomplete disclosure
Process may be more expensive than mediation

blocks.conclusion_template: Cohabitation by the spousal support recipient with a new partner may constitute grounds for reduction or termination of support. The standard varies by jurisdiction: some require a showing of economic benefit from the cohabitation relationship, others terminate support automatically upon cohabitation. In Texas, cohabitation in a dating or conjugal relationship on a continuing basis is grounds for termination. Courts examine the nature of the relationship, shared expenses, financial interdependence, and public perception.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. DEFINITION: What constitutes cohabitation under applicable law? 2. EVIDENCE: Shared residence, financial interdependence, romantic relationship. 3. ECONOMIC BENEFIT: Does cohabitation reduce recipient's financial need? 4. AUTOMATIC vs DISCRETIONARY: Does cohabitation automatically terminate or trigger review? 5. BURDEN: Who bears the burden of proving cohabitation? 6. CONTRACTUAL: Does the support agreement address cohabitation?
key_factors: Whether support order or agreement addresses cohabitation

primary_authority.relevance: NJ cohabitation rebuttable presumption of reduced need
CA rebuttable presumption of decreased need on cohabitation

counter_arguments: Cohabitation may not actually reduce financial need
Definition of cohabitation is vague
Surveillance to prove cohabitation raises privacy concerns
Automatic termination may be harsh if cohabitation is brief

blocks.conclusion_template: Marital debts are divided along with assets in divorce. In community property states, debts incurred during marriage for the benefit of the community are community obligations. In equitable distribution states, debts are allocated based on factors similar to property division. Critically, property settlement agreements do not bind creditors — if one spouse is ordered to pay a joint debt and defaults, the creditor may pursue the other spouse. Indemnification provisions and hold-harmless clauses provide contractual protection but not creditor protection.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. CHARACTERIZATION: Is the debt community/marital or separate? 2. TIMING: Was the debt incurred during the marriage? 3. PURPOSE: Was the debt for the benefit of the community/marriage? 4. ALLOCATION: Divide debts equitably, often with the asset they encumber. 5. CREDITOR RIGHTS: Assignment does not affect creditor rights against both parties. 6. INDEMNIFICATION: Include hold-harmless provisions for protection.
key_factors: Whether debt was incurred during marriage
Which spouse benefited from the debt
Whether debt is secured by marital asset
Ability of each party to pay

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Feldman, 153 Cal.App.4th 1470 (2007)
primary_authority.relevance: Debt characterization and division in California
Non-dischargeability of divorce debt allocation in bankruptcy

primary_authority.reference: Tedder v. Gardner Aldrich, LLP, 421 S.W.3d 651 (Tex. 2013)

counter_arguments: Property settlement does not bind creditors creating ongoing exposure
Bankruptcy may discharge obligation to pay assigned debt
Student loan characterization varies by jurisdiction
Tax debt allocation follows different rules

blocks.conclusion_template: Whether a professional license or degree is marital/community property is highly jurisdiction-dependent. New York (O'Brien) treats enhanced earning capacity as marital property subject to equitable distribution. Most other states reject this approach, instead providing reimbursement for the supporting spouse's contributions. In community property states, community funds spent on education may be subject to reimbursement. The trend is away from treating degrees as divisible property and toward compensating the supporting spouse through alimony or equitable division of other assets.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. JURISDICTION: Does the state treat licenses/degrees as marital property? 2. IF PROPERTY: Calculate present value of enhanced earning capacity (O'Brien method). 3. IF NOT PROPERTY: Calculate reimbursement for community funds spent on education. 4. SPOUSAL SUPPORT: Consider supporting spouse's contribution in alimony determination. 5. EVIDENCE: Expert testimony on enhanced earning capacity. 6. ALTERNATIVE REMEDY: Disproportionate property division or extended alimony.
key_factors: Whether jurisdiction treats degree as marital property
Duration of marriage relative to education
Whether supporting spouse benefited from enhanced income

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Graham, 194 Colo. 429 (1978)
primary_authority.relevance: Degree is not marital property (majority view)

counter_arguments: Degrees cannot be sold or transferred like property
Enhanced earning capacity calculation is speculative
Reimbursement may not adequately compensate supporting spouse
Future earning capacity is not guaranteed

blocks.conclusion_template: Reimbursement claims arise when one estate (community or separate) benefits another estate. In Texas, economic contribution claims (Tex. Fam. Code 3.402-3.410) address community funds used to pay down separate property debt, and vice versa. The claim is measured by the reduction in principal on the debt, not the total payments made (which include interest). Reimbursement is equitable, not automatic — the court considers offset and whether the benefit was intended as a gift.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. IDENTIFY BENEFIT: Which estate benefited from which estate's funds? 2. MEASURE: Calculate principal reduction, not total payments. 3. OFFSET: Was there an offsetting benefit (e.g., rent-free use of separate property home)? 4. GIFT: Was the contribution intended as a gift? Gift negates reimbursement. 5. EQUITY: Court has discretion to award or deny reimbursement based on equity.
key_factors: Whether contribution was intended as gift

primary_authority.relevance: Reimbursement for community contributions to separate estate
California reimbursement for separate property contributions

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Walrath, 17 Cal.4th 907 (1998)

counter_arguments: Tracing contributions over long marriages is difficult
Gift presumption may defeat legitimate claims
Offset calculations are subjective
Principal-only measurement may understate true contribution

blocks.conclusion_template: The date of separation determines when community property accumulation ceases and affects property characterization, support calculations, and filing deadlines. In California, the date of separation requires a complete and final break evidenced by objective conduct. In Texas, there is no formal separation concept — community property continues until final divorce decree. The date is frequently contested because it affects classification of assets and debts acquired between separation and divorce.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. DEFINITION: How does the jurisdiction define separation? 2. EVIDENCE: Objective conduct showing complete break (separate residences, filed divorce, separate finances). 3. IMPACT: On property characterization, support, filing deadlines. 4. LIVING TOGETHER: Can parties be separated while living under the same roof? (Some jurisdictions yes). 5. RECONCILIATION: Does reconciliation restart the community? 6. TEXAS: No formal separation — community continues until decree.
key_factors: Whether divorce was filed or contemplated
Objective evidence of intent to end marriage
Impact on specific asset or debt classification

primary_authority.reference: In re Marriage of Davis, 61 Cal.4th 846 (2015)
primary_authority.relevance: Objective evidence required for date of separation (CA)
Texas community continues until divorce decree
NY one-year separation ground for divorce

counter_arguments: Parties may disagree on when separation occurred
Living under same roof complicates determination
Reconciliation attempts may reset the date
In Texas absence of separation concept creates extended community period

blocks.conclusion_template: Postnuptial agreements are contracts between spouses during marriage that alter property rights. In Texas, spouses may partition community property or convert separate to community (and vice versa) by written agreement. Postnuptial agreements face heightened scrutiny compared to prenuptial agreements because of the fiduciary relationship between spouses. Requirements include full disclosure, voluntary execution, fair terms, and in some jurisdictions, independent counsel for both parties.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. AUTHORITY: Does the jurisdiction allow postnuptial agreements? 2. FIDUCIARY DUTY: Spouses owe each other heightened duty of disclosure. 3. DISCLOSURE: Full and fair financial disclosure required. 4. VOLUNTARINESS: Free from duress, coercion, or overreaching. 5. FAIRNESS: Terms must be fair and equitable at execution. 6. INDEPENDENT COUNSEL: Recommended or required for both parties.
key_factors: Full financial disclosure by both parties
Whether both parties had independent counsel

primary_authority.relevance: Texas partition and exchange agreement provisions

primary_authority.reference: Uniform Premarital and Marital Agreements Act (UPMAA) § 9

counter_arguments: Fiduciary duty makes arms-length negotiation difficult
Agreements during marital crisis may be coercive
Consideration issues arise since marriage already exists
Enforceability is less certain than prenuptial agreements

blocks.conclusion_template: A child's preference regarding custody is a relevant factor but not determinative. In Texas, children 12 and older have the right to express a preference to the court by interview in chambers. The court gives the preference appropriate weight based on the child's age, maturity, understanding of the situation, and whether the preference appears freely given or coached. The child's preference does not override the best interest standard. In some jurisdictions, the judge must interview the child if requested; in others, it is discretionary.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. AGE THRESHOLD: Does the child meet the minimum age for preference (12 in TX, varies elsewhere)? 2. MATURITY: Is the child mature enough for a reliable preference? 3. FREE WILL: Is the preference freely given or result of coaching/alienation? 4. REASON: What is the basis for the child's preference? 5. WEIGHT: Preference is one factor, not controlling. 6. PROCEDURE: In chambers interview, often without parties present.
key_factors: Whether coaching or alienation is suspected

primary_authority.relevance: Interview of child 12 or older regarding preference
Weight given to child's preference in Texas
Child's preference as factor in custody

counter_arguments: Young children's preferences may reflect manipulation
Child may choose the permissive parent over the structured one
Interview process may traumatize child
Child's current preference may not reflect long-term best interest

blocks.conclusion_template: Expert witnesses play critical roles in family law proceedings: custody evaluators assess parenting capacity and make recommendations, forensic psychologists evaluate mental health and abuse allegations, vocational experts determine earning capacity for imputation and rehabilitative support, business appraisers value closely held businesses and professional practices, and actuaries value pension and retirement benefits. Expert selection, qualification, and cross-examination are essential litigation skills. Daubert/Robinson standards apply to expert testimony admissibility.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. NEED: What issue requires expert testimony? 2. TYPE: Which type of expert is appropriate? 3. QUALIFICATION: Does the expert meet Daubert/Robinson standards? 4. METHODOLOGY: Is the expert's methodology reliable and accepted? 5. OPINION: Is the opinion supported by the facts? 6. CROSS-EXAMINATION: Identify weaknesses in methodology and opinions.
key_factors: Type of expert needed for the issue
Whether opinion is supported by facts

primary_authority.reference: Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, 509 U.S. 579 (1993)
E.I. du Pont v. Robinson, 923 S.W.2d 549 (Tex. 1995)
APA Guidelines for Child Custody Evaluations (2010)

counter_arguments: Expert opinions are inherently subjective in family law context
Dueling experts confuse rather than clarify issues
Cost of experts creates access to justice concerns
Custody evaluation methodology lacks standardization

blocks.conclusion_template: Discovery in family law includes interrogatories, requests for production, depositions, subpoenas to third parties, and jurisdiction-specific tools like sworn inventories and appraisements. In Texas, each party must file a sworn inventory and appraisement of all property. Discovery is essential for property characterization, income determination, and hidden asset identification. Proportionality and good faith requirements apply. Discovery abuse may result in sanctions including adverse inferences, fee awards, and striking pleadings.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. MANDATORY DISCLOSURE: Sworn inventory, financial declarations, UCCJEA declaration. 2. WRITTEN DISCOVERY: Interrogatories and requests for production. 3. ORAL DISCOVERY: Depositions of parties and third parties. 4. SUBPOENAS: Financial institutions, employers, business records. 5. DIGITAL: Social media, email, text messages, app data. 6. SANCTIONS: For failure to disclose or discovery abuse.

primary_authority.relevance: Texas discovery rules applicable to family cases
Discovery abuse sanctions in family cases
California fiduciary duty of disclosure in divorce

counter_arguments: Discovery costs may be disproportionate to estate value
Digital evidence raises privacy concerns
Discovery abuse is common and enforcement inconsistent
Privilege claims may shield relevant information

blocks.topic: Domestic Relations Exception to Federal Jurisdiction
blocks.conclusion_template: The domestic relations exception bars federal courts from exercising diversity jurisdiction over cases involving divorce, alimony, or child custody, even when diversity of citizenship and amount-in-controversy requirements are met. The exception is narrowly construed — federal courts may hear tort actions between spouses, contract disputes arising from divorce settlements, and constitutional claims affecting family law (e.g., Troxel, Obergefell). The Rooker-Feldman doctrine separately bars federal review of state family court judgments.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. EXCEPTION SCOPE: Does the claim seek divorce, alimony, or custody? If so, barred from federal court. 2. NARROW CONSTRUCTION: Claims collateral to domestic relations (torts, contracts, constitutional) may proceed. 3. ABSTENTION: Even if not barred, federal courts may abstain under Younger or Burford. 4. ROOKER-FELDMAN: Federal courts cannot review state court family law judgments. 5. CONSTITUTIONAL CLAIMS: 1983 actions, due process, equal protection claims may proceed.
key_factors: Whether claim directly involves divorce, alimony, or custody
Whether claim is collateral to domestic relations
Whether state court judgment is being challenged

primary_authority.relevance: Scope of domestic relations exception to federal jurisdiction
Narrow scope of probate/domestic relations exception

primary_authority.reference: Rooker-Feldman doctrine (D.C. Ct. App. v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983))
primary_authority.relevance: Federal courts cannot review state court judgments

counter_arguments: Exception's scope is uncertain for claims tangential to domestic relations
Federal courts may be better forum for constitutional claims
Abstention gives state courts monopoly even on federal claims
Exception is judicially created, not statutory

blocks.conclusion_template: Covenant marriage is an optional legal marriage framework available in Louisiana, Arizona, and Arkansas that requires premarital counseling and limits grounds for divorce to fault-based causes (adultery, abuse, abandonment, felony conviction, substance abuse) or extended separation (typically 2 years). Couples choosing covenant marriage agree to seek counseling before filing for divorce. The covenant limits no-fault divorce options. Courts in non-covenant states must give full faith and credit to covenant marriages but may apply their own divorce standards.
blocks.reasoning_framework: 1. AVAILABILITY: Is the marriage a covenant marriage? Only in LA, AZ, AR. 2. GROUNDS: Limited to fault grounds or extended separation. 3. COUNSELING: Pre-divorce counseling is required before filing. 4. FULL FAITH AND CREDIT: Other states recognize but may apply own standards. 5. CONVERSION: Can a standard marriage be converted to covenant? (Yes in covenant states).
key_factors: Whether marriage is designated as covenant
Available grounds for divorce under covenant law
Which state is adjudicating the divorce
Whether conversion from standard marriage occurred

primary_authority.reference: Spaht, 'Louisiana's Covenant Marriage Law,' 12 Regent U. L. Rev. 192 (1999)

counter_arguments: Covenant marriage restricts individual autonomy
Fault requirements may trap spouses in unhappy marriages
Very low adoption rate suggests limited public support
Full faith and credit issues when litigating in non-covenant state
